observations.text: Sale items (marked with a red tag) are final sale and are not eligible for return or exchange for any reason.
Items that arrive damaged or defective may be returned within 14 days of delivery for a full refund or replacement, regardless of item condition upon return.
Standard-price items may be returned within 30 days of delivery for a full refund, provided the item is unused and in its original packaging.
Refunds are issued to the original payment method within 5-7 business days of us receiving the returned item.

definitions.text: Per the policy's parenthetical, a 'sale item' is one marked with a red tag. The user's item is described as a red-tag sale item, so it falls within the class addressed by clause 2.
Clause 3 addresses items that 'arrive damaged or defective' — i.e., damage present at delivery rather than caused later by the buyer. Damage occurring in shipping is damage present on arrival.

assumptions.text: The item was delivered on or around the date of purchase 10 days ago, so it is within 14 days of delivery.
assumptions.why_needed: Both clauses 2 and 3 count time from delivery, but the user gave a purchase date ('bought ... 10 days ago'), not a delivery date. If delivery lagged purchase, the item is even more comfortably inside 14 days; if the user misremembered and delivery was earlier, the window could matter. Needed to evaluate the timing element at all.

assumptions.text: No assumption is made about which of clause 2 and clause 3 prevails; the knowledge base is treated as silent on their interaction.
assumptions.why_needed: Clause 2 excludes red-tag items from return 'for any reason'; clause 3 permits return of damaged items with no stated exception for sale items. Both apply to this exact situation and the policy never states a precedence rule. Silently choosing one would fabricate a rule the source does not contain.

backed_claims.text: The item falls simultaneously within the scope of clause 2 (red-tag sale item) and clause 3 (arrived damaged, within 14 days of delivery).
backed_claims.falsification_path: Show the item was not red-tagged, or that the damage was buyer-caused after delivery rather than present on arrival, or that delivery occurred more than 14 days ago.

backed_claims.text: The policy as written does not resolve the conflict: it contains no precedence clause, no 'except' language in clause 3 carving out sale items, and no 'notwithstanding' language in clause 2 yielding to clause 3.
backed_claims.falsification_path: Point to any text in the policy establishing precedence between clauses, or an exception in either clause referencing the other.

backed_claims.text: Clause 1's condition requirements (unused, original packaging) are not an obstacle here, because clause 3 explicitly waives return condition and clause 1 applies to standard-price items.
backed_claims.falsification_path: Show that clause 1's conditions are intended to apply to all returns including damaged-item returns.

backed_claims.text: If the return is accepted, the refund would go to the original payment method within 5-7 business days of the retailer receiving the item.
backed_claims.falsification_path: A separate policy term excluding sale items or damaged-item returns from the standard refund mechanics.

unverified_claims.text: Damage-on-arrival overrides final-sale status, so the return is permitted.
'Final sale ... for any reason' is absolute and defeats the damaged-goods clause, so the return is refused.
The retailer has any obligation outside this policy (e.g. statutory consumer protection, carrier shipping-damage claims) that would independently entitle the buyer to a refund.

hypotheses.text: Proceeding on the reading that clause 3 governs, because it is the more specific provision (it addresses a narrow factual trigger — damage on arrival — and expressly overrides an otherwise-general return condition, 'regardless of item condition upon return'), while clause 2 states a general status-based bar. Under this reading the refund is owed.
hypotheses.falsification_path: A retailer ruling, an order-page disclaimer, or a policy version stating that final-sale status applies even to damaged goods; or confirmation from Northgate that clause 2 is intended as an absolute bar. Conversely, confirmation that clause 3 has no sale-item exception would support it.

hypotheses.text: The phrase 'for any reason' in clause 2 was drafted to defeat buyer-preference reasons (changed mind, wrong size, fit) rather than to disclaim liability for goods damaged before the buyer ever received them.
hypotheses.falsification_path: Evidence of drafting intent or prior enforcement showing Northgate has refused damaged-on-arrival red-tag returns.

conclusion.text: The policy as written does not settle your case — it collides with itself. Your item is squarely covered by two clauses at once: clause 2 says red-tag sale items are 'not eligible for return or exchange for any reason,' and clause 3 says items that arrive damaged may be returned within 14 days for a full refund or replacement, with no stated exception for sale items. You are inside the 14-day window (assuming delivery was at/near your purchase date 10 days ago), and clause 3 expressly waives any condition-on-return requirement, so nothing else blocks you. The policy contains no precedence rule, so I cannot tell you definitively which clause wins. My working read — flagged as a hypothesis, not a backed answer — is that clause 3 should govern, since it is the specific damaged-on-arrival carve-out and already overrides other general conditions, whereas clause 2 is a general status bar most naturally aimed at buyer's-remorse returns. On that read you would get a full refund or replacement, issued to your original payment method 5-7 business days after they receive the item. But you should get Northgate to confirm which clause they apply, because a reading where 'for any reason' is absolute is equally available on this text.
